notes.made: Paddy McAloon wrote it in 1984, one of his first songs on a keyboard, over a hip-hop-type groove on a drum machine. Thomas Dolby produced Steve McQueen, rehearsing the band at Nomis in West London and recording at Marcus Studios, and he plays the synth intro here. He worked out the bass with Martin McAloon by having him sing lines from other songs, Dobie Gray's 'The "In" Crowd' among them, to remember the rhythms. McAloon called Dolby 'a junior Quincy Jones' in a 1985 interview.
notes.context: Kitchenware released the album on 22 June 1985 and this as its third single in August. It got to 92. Steve McQueen reached 21 and NME made it their fourth album of the year, which tells you where Prefab Sprout lived in 1985: adored by critics, ignored by the chart, with a song about a pregnant girl who wants to name her child after everything good in her life.

listen_for.note: That's Dolby himself on the synth intro.
A rolling arpeggiated synth comes in, and soft pads shadow Wendy Smith's backing vocals so her voice seems to widen.
McAloon's own description: bass and drums 'locked together in a beautiful pattern', with counterpoint running through every part. Dolby built most of it.

leads_to.title: The 'In' Crowd
leads_to.why: Martin McAloon sang this to himself to keep the bass rhythm in his head, so a piece of 60s soul is hiding in the bottom end.

notes.unverified: Rafe's quote about the harmony stacks being 'the most careful pop arranging of the decade' is opinion. Thomas Dolby himself felt he didn't do the song justice, per Wikipedia.

culture.title: Number 92
culture.line: Released in August 1985 as the third single from Steve McQueen, it reached 92 over two non-consecutive weeks. NME named the album its fourth best of the year.
